How to use this method volume

rows: Part 2 cue-card families, TA hybrid storytelling, one-minute planning, expanded stage-by-stage phrase banks, Part 3 reasoning frameworks, and one fully worked linked topic with three Part-2 and eighteen Part-3 model answers.
File 2 covers Sets 1–20; File 3 covers Sets 21–40; File 4 covers Sets 41–60. Each set links one Part-2 cue card to two related Part-3 question groups.

blocks.text: Design principle Part 2 and Part 3 share a theme, but they test different modes of speaking. Part 2 is personal storytelling; Part 3 moves outward to society, causes, comparisons, evaluation and speculation. The transition must feel natural rather than like two unrelated lessons.
PART 1 · Test Logic and Band-9 Targets

rows: Prepare for 1 minute; speak for up to 2 minutes on a cue card.
A vivid personal story with a clear flow, selective details, emotional movement and a natural reflection.
Discuss broader and more abstract issues related to Part 2.
A natural discussion: direct position → explanation → example → nuance, without sounding like an essay read aloud.

blocks.text: Shared Band-9 standard Fluency is not speed. High-level performance sounds easy to follow, uses vocabulary precisely, moves flexibly across time and possibility, and uses stress/intonation to make meaning clear.
PART 2 · Speaking Part 2 Method
2.1 Five common cue-card families

rows: Identity, relationship, defining quality, one revealing incident, impact on you.
Location, first/typical visit, sensory snapshot, activities, emotional meaning.
Origin, appearance/function, how you use/experienced it, story, significance.

blocks.text: TA four-part flow ANCHOR (what/who) → SCENE (when/where/why) → 2–3 SELECTED DETAILS with reactions → REFLECTION / wish. Aim for about 230–260 words at a relaxed pace.
2.3 One-minute note-taking

rows: Choose the real story or reusable story module.
Write 4–6 keywords: scene, turning point, strongest details.
Add two feeling words and one high-value phrase.
Choose final reflection; check all cue points are coverable.

blocks.text: Do not write sentences Notes should trigger speech, not become a script. Example: “Kichi — 10 yrs — conveyor — spicy broth — kid sick — manager tactful — looked after”.

blocks.text: PART 3 · Speaking Part 3 Method
3.1 Eight common question types

rows: Do you think…? Is it a good idea…?
Take a position; justify; acknowledge limits.
One main cause, mechanism and example; add a secondary cause only if useful.
How are A and B different? Which is better?
Use a clear comparison dimension: cost, age, access, motivation, impact.
Past baseline → driver of change → present consequence.
Prioritize, explain and weigh; do not merely list.
What problems…? What should be done?
Specific actor + feasible action + expected result + limitation.
What will happen in the future?
Use probability, evidence and conditional consequences.
State likely effect, explain chain and add nuance/exception.

blocks.text: 3.2 The TA Part 3 formula

rows: Buy a moment and frame complexity.
“I think it depends, really.” / “Not necessarily.” / “That is a tricky one.”
Give the listener a clear position.
“The main reason is…” / “On balance, I would say…”
Show why/how through a logical chain.
“That is largely because…” / “which in turn means…”
Use a short real-world or hypothetical example.
“A good example would be…” / “Take urban workers, for instance…”
Limit the claim or show another side.
“That said,…” / “Of course, this varies…” / “So it is not entirely straightforward.”

blocks.text: Length target Develop one answer for roughly 35–60 seconds. One well-explained reason plus an example often sounds more advanced than three undeveloped points.
3.3 Useful language by reasoning function

rows: I would say yes and no. / In principle…, but in practice… / It depends largely on…
This tends to stem from… / One major factor is… / That is partly driven by…
which in turn leads to… / The knock-on effect is… / Over time, this can…
The key difference lies in… / Compared with… / A is more likely to…, whereas B…
Take…, for instance. / A simple example is… / This is particularly clear in…
I can imagine… / It is quite likely that… / We may see… / I doubt that…
The most practical step would be… / Governments could… / This would only work if…
That is not to say… / There are exceptions, of course. / Beyond a certain point,…

blocks.text: 3.4 What to avoid
Essay openings such as “There are several reasons for this phenomenon” when a natural spoken opening would be clearer.
Mechanical three-point lists with no explanation.
Overconfident generalisations about “all young people”, “the government” or “society”.
Personal Part-2 storytelling when the Part-3 question asks about people in general.
Forcing memorised idioms or overly formal vocabulary that does not match spoken interaction.
PART 4 · Complete Linked Topic
Topic — RESTAURANTS & FOOD CULTURE
Part 2 cue card
Describe a restaurant you enjoy going to.
where it is
when you first went there
what the restaurant and food are like
and explain why you enjoy going there
One-minute TA notes Kichi-Kichi — 5 mins from home — first visit 10+ yrs — conveyor belt — spicy broth / octopus — child sick — manager tactful — “felt looked after”.
TA — refined Band-9 model

When I hear this question, Kichi-Kichi is the first place that springs to mind. It is a hot-pot chain, and the branch we usually go to is only about five minutes from my house in Bình Thạnh, so it has become our default choice whenever nobody feels like cooking.
I first went there over a decade ago with my wife, when the conveyor-belt concept was still fairly new in Viet Nam. We were both curious because, instead of walking around with a plate, you sit at your table and small dishes of beef, seafood, mushrooms and vegetables glide past you. It is a little like shopping for food without leaving your chair, which suits me perfectly.
Food-wise, I normally choose a spicy soup base and then completely lose track of how much octopus and beef I have eaten. The price is slightly on the high side, but the ingredients are fresh and there is enough variety to keep everyone happy, including my children.
What really won me over, though, was the service. On one visit, one of my kids suddenly felt sick and made a terrible mess. My wife and I were mortified, but the manager handled it with such tact: she reassured us, arranged another table and had everything cleaned without making us feel awkward.
That small act of kindness stayed with me. Plenty of restaurants serve good food; this one made us feel looked after, which is why we keep going back.

Why this works The answer follows one central story rather than four isolated cues. Concrete food details create imagery, the service incident gives the talk a turning point, and the final contrast (“good food” versus “felt looked after”) provides a memorable reflection.
Alternative A — family-run local restaurant

I would like to talk about a tiny family-run restaurant in Quy Nhon called Bếp Nhà Mình, which roughly means “our home kitchen.” It is tucked away in a side street near the beach, so most tourists walk straight past it, but local people seem to know it very well.
I discovered it during a short holiday with two friends. We had spent the afternoon at the beach and were looking for somewhere unpretentious to eat. The restaurant had plastic stools, handwritten menus and an open kitchen where an elderly couple were cooking together. It did not look impressive in the usual Instagram sense, but the smell coming from the kitchen made the decision for us.
We ordered grilled squid, steamed fish and a bowl of sour soup. Everything tasted remarkably fresh, particularly the squid, which had probably been caught that morning. The owner also kept bringing us small extras — herbs, fruit and a homemade dipping sauce — while insisting that we needed to eat more because we looked tired.
What made the meal memorable was not just the food but the atmosphere. There was no polished service or elaborate décor; it felt as though we had been invited into someone’s home. We ended up chatting with the owners about the town and stayed far longer than planned.
I have eaten in much fancier places, but very few have felt that warm. It reminded me that hospitality is often more memorable than presentation, and I would return without hesitation.
Alternative B — rooftop café

The place I have in mind is a rooftop café called The Workshop, located on the upper floor of an old building in central Ho Chi Minh City. You have to walk through a slightly gloomy entrance and climb several flights of stairs, so the first visit feels almost like searching for a secret room.
A colleague introduced me to it a few years ago when we needed somewhere quiet to discuss a project. Once the door opened, the contrast was striking: high ceilings, large windows, lots of natural light and a calm view over the busy streets below. The menu is fairly simple, mainly coffee, pastries and light meals, but everything is carefully prepared.
I usually order a flat white and a toasted sandwich. Neither is cheap, but the coffee is consistently good and, more importantly, nobody rushes you. There are long communal tables for people working on laptops and smaller corners where friends can talk without competing with loud music.
What I enjoy most is the feeling of being removed from the city without actually leaving it. Downstairs, traffic is roaring and people are hurrying in every direction; upstairs, time seems to slow down. I have written lesson plans there, met friends and occasionally sat alone with a book.
It is not the kind of café I visit every day, but whenever I need a change of scene and a little mental space, it is one of the first places I think of.
Part 3 — Set A: Restaurants and eating out
1. Why do people choose restaurants for celebrations?

TA — refined Partly because a restaurant turns an ordinary meal into an occasion. Nobody has to shop, cook or clear up afterwards, so the hosts can actually spend time with their guests. It also solves the space problem, especially in cities where homes may be too small for a large family gathering. That said, the restaurant is really just the setting; what people remember is usually the conversation and the feeling of being together.

Alternative A Restaurants provide a neutral space that feels more special than someone’s dining room. The change of setting encourages people to dress up, order food they would not normally cook and take photographs, so the event feels clearly separated from everyday life. For milestones such as graduations or anniversaries, that sense of ceremony can matter as much as the food itself.

Alternative B There is also a practical reason: restaurants can cater for different ages and preferences. At a family celebration, one person may want seafood, another may be vegetarian and the children may only eat something simple. A good restaurant can handle all of that without placing the entire burden on one family member, which makes the event far less stressful.
Quick analysis Each answer develops a different reasoning route so students can compare ideas rather than memorize a single “correct” opinion.
2. Why are fast-food restaurants popular with some groups?

TA — refined I think the biggest attractions are speed, predictability and price. Students or office workers often have limited time, and at a fast-food outlet they know roughly what the meal will cost and how it will taste. The downside is that convenience can easily become a habit. Traditional food may be healthier and more varied, but it usually requires more time, either to prepare or to sit down and enjoy properly.

Alternative A Delivery apps have made fast food even more accessible. A customer can place an order in seconds, track it and receive a discounted meal without leaving home. That system fits modern urban life extremely well, particularly for younger people. Its popularity is therefore not only about the food; it is also about a highly efficient way of buying it.

Alternative B I would not say fast food is universally more popular. In Viet Nam, inexpensive local meals such as phở or cơm tấm can be just as quick and often taste fresher. International fast-food chains appeal because they are familiar and heavily marketed, but in many neighborhoods, traditional eateries still win on value, variety and cultural attachment.
Quick analysis Each answer develops a different reasoning route so students can compare ideas rather than memorize a single “correct” opinion.
3. Is food in expensive restaurants always better?

TA — refined Not necessarily. A high bill may reflect the location, interior design, service staff and even the reputation of the chef rather than a dramatic difference in taste. I have had excellent street food for a few dollars and fairly forgettable meals in elegant dining rooms. Expensive restaurants can offer better ingredients and more technical cooking, but price is only a rough signal of quality, not a guarantee.

Alternative A There is often a reason for the higher price. Premium restaurants may source seasonal ingredients, employ highly trained chefs and spend hours preparing a single sauce or dish. Diners are also paying for consistency and service. Even so, personal taste is subjective, so a perfectly executed dish can still be less enjoyable to someone than the simple food they grew up eating.

Alternative B I think there are diminishing returns. Moving from very cheap food to a good mid-range restaurant can produce a noticeable improvement in freshness and service. Moving from an expensive restaurant to an extremely expensive one may only add tiny refinements. For most people, the best meal is where quality, atmosphere and price feel balanced rather than where the bill is highest.
Quick analysis Each answer develops a different reasoning route so students can compare ideas rather than memorize a single “correct” opinion.
Part 3 — Set B: Food culture and the restaurant industry
4. What qualities make a restaurant successful?

TA — refined Consistency comes first. A restaurant may attract people once through advertising or attractive décor, but customers only return if the food is reliably good. Service and hygiene are equally important because one careless interaction or visibly dirty table can destroy trust immediately. The strongest restaurants usually do a few things well, understand who their customers are and make the whole experience feel effortless.

Alternative A A clear identity is crucial. Some places succeed because they serve one regional dish brilliantly; others offer a distinctive atmosphere or a very specific dining experience. Problems arise when a restaurant tries to satisfy everyone and ends up with an enormous menu but no real strength. Customers should be able to explain in one sentence why that restaurant is worth visiting.

Alternative B Value matters more than simply being cheap. People are willing to pay a premium when the ingredients, portion size, service and setting justify it. Online reputation also matters enormously now. A restaurant can recover from one negative review, but repeated complaints about the same issue — slow service, poor hygiene or misleading photos — will quickly drive customers elsewhere.
Quick analysis Notice the natural opening, one dominant argument, a concrete illustration and a final qualification.
5. Should restaurants serve only local food?

TA — refined No, I think that would make food culture unnecessarily narrow. Restaurants should preserve local dishes and ingredients, particularly in tourist areas, but diners also benefit from having access to other cuisines. In fact, foreign food can encourage local chefs to experiment and improve. The sensible balance is to protect authenticity where it matters while still allowing variety and thoughtful fusion.

Alternative A In places that depend heavily on tourism, local food should probably be given greater prominence. Visitors often want to understand a region through what it eats, and restaurants can support farmers, fishing communities and traditional recipes. That does not mean banning foreign dishes, but a town loses something valuable if every central street is dominated by the same international chains.

Alternative B Restaurants respond to the people living around them. In a diverse city, serving only local food would ignore immigrant communities and changing tastes. Cuisine has always developed through contact and exchange anyway. Many dishes now considered traditional contain ingredients or techniques that originally came from elsewhere, so drawing a strict line between “local” and “foreign” is harder than it sounds.
Quick analysis Notice the natural opening, one dominant argument, a concrete illustration and a final qualification.
6. How has food culture changed in your country?

TA — refined Eating out has become far more routine in Viet Nam. In the past, restaurant meals were often reserved for celebrations, whereas many urban families now eat out or order delivery several times a week. People are also exposed to a much wider range of cuisines. At the same time, expectations have risen: diners pay closer attention to hygiene, presentation, online reviews and the overall experience, not just whether the food is filling.

Alternative A One noticeable change is greater interest in health. Traditional meals were not automatically healthy, but they often included fresh vegetables and fairly simple ingredients. Modern consumers now talk about calories, protein, organic produce and plant-based options. This is positive, although health labels can also become a marketing device, so people still need to look beyond the fashionable language.

Alternative B Food has become more social and visual. People choose restaurants partly because the setting photographs well, and a meal may appear online before anyone has actually tasted it. That can help small businesses reach customers, but it also encourages novelty over substance. I suspect the most successful places will be those that look appealing without forgetting that people eventually come back for flavor and hospitality.
